overview.text: Italy is a republic in southern Europe with Rome as its capital. The modern Italian state grew from nineteenth-century unification: the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in 1861. In 1922, after the Fascist March on Rome, King Victor Emmanuel III appointed Benito Mussolini prime minister. Fascist rule became a dictatorship that suppressed other parties and press freedom; Mussolini fell from power in 1943. After World War II, voters chose a republic over a monarchy in a 1946 referendum, and the new constitution took effect in 1948. Later, political violence marked the Years of Lead, including the 1969 Piazza Fontana bombing and the Red Brigades’ 1978 kidnapping and murder of Aldo Moro.

The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in 1861.
The king appointed Mussolini prime minister after the March on Rome in 1922.
A 1946 referendum chose a republic; the constitution took effect in 1948.
The Piazza Fontana bombing in 1969 was an early event in the Years of Lead.
The Red Brigades kidnapped and murdered Aldo Moro in 1978.

overview.text: Denmark is a Scandinavian country whose European territory consists of the Jutland Peninsula and many islands, including Zealand, where Copenhagen stands. The wider Kingdom of Denmark also includes Greenland and the Faroe Islands. Those two territories have extensive self-government, so describing them simply as colonies obscures their present political status. Danish authorities retain responsibility for foreign policy under the kingdom’s constitutional arrangements. Denmark once ruled Caribbean islands called the Danish West Indies; it transferred St. Thomas, St. John, and St. Croix to the United States in 1917. The country is a constitutional monarchy with a parliament called the Folketing, while Greenland and the Faroes have their own political institutions.

European Denmark includes Jutland and hundreds of islands.
Greenland and the Faroe Islands are part of the wider Kingdom of Denmark.
The Faroes gained home rule in 1948 and Greenland in 1979.

overview.text: The Kingdom of Denmark under Valdemar IV Atterdag was a medieval state being rebuilt after years without a king and the mortgaging of much of its territory. Valdemar became king in 1340 and used taxation, negotiation, and warfare to reclaim lands. He sold Danish Estonia to the Teutonic Order in 1346 and took Gotland, including the trading town of Visby, in 1361. His expansion threatened the Hanseatic towns that traded around the Baltic Sea. A broad coalition fought Denmark, and the 1370 peace at Stralsund gave the Hanseatic League control of the Skåne fairs for fifteen years. Valdemar’s reign ended in 1375, before the later Kalmar Union.

overview.text: Rajiv Gandhi was India’s prime minister from 1984 to 1989. He was the son of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi and grandson of Jawaharlal Nehru, independent India’s first prime minister. A commercial airline pilot before entering politics, he took office after his mother was assassinated in 1984. His government signed the 1987 Indo-Lanka Accord with Sri Lanka, intended to address the island’s ethnic conflict and to arrange political changes there. The agreement contemplated Indian military assistance if Sri Lanka requested it. Gandhi lost power in 1989. During an election campaign in Tamil Nadu on May 21, 1991, a suicide bomber killed him at Sriperumbudur in a plot linked to the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam.

Before politics, he was a pilot with Indian Airlines.

overview.text: The Mexican Revolution began in 1910 as a challenge to the long rule of Porfirio Díaz. Francisco I. Madero called for an uprising, while movements in different regions demanded political change, land, and workers’ rights. Díaz resigned in 1911, but the conflict did not end with his departure. Emiliano Zapata and Francisco Villa became major revolutionary leaders, and rival factions later fought one another. Venustiano Carranza’s constitutionalist forces prevailed over the conventionist coalition and called a constituent congress. The resulting Constitution of 1917 addressed education, land and subsoil rights, local government, labor, and relations between church and state. The revolution reshaped Mexico for years beyond its initial uprising.

overview.text: The agoge was the public system of upbringing and training associated with the citizen class of ancient Sparta. Boys destined for Spartan citizenship entered group training at a young age, learning discipline, endurance, cooperation, and habits useful in war. A public supervisor and older youths helped direct them. The system connected military preparation with the formation of adult citizens and their loyalty to the community. Ancient writers such as Xenophon credited its rules to Lycurgus, but the historical existence and exact date of that lawgiver are uncertain. Spartan society also included helots and other noncitizens; the agoge should not be mistaken for schooling shared equally by everyone living under Spartan rule.

key_facts.text: The agoge trained boys of Sparta’s citizen class.
Ancient sources associated the system with Lycurgus.
Training emphasized endurance, discipline, and preparation for military service.
Boys trained in age groups under public supervision.
Helots were a distinct subjugated population, not equal participants in citizen training.
Lycurgus’s historical identity and dates are uncertain.

overview.text: England is one of the four constituent countries of the United Kingdom, alongside Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland. It is part of the island of Great Britain, a geographic name that also includes Scotland and Wales. England has its own long history, but it is no longer a separate sovereign kingdom. The Norman victory at Hastings in 1066 changed its rulers and institutions. Centuries later, the rival houses of Lancaster and York fought for the English crown in the Wars of the Roses. In 1707, the English and Scottish kingdoms united to form Great Britain and a single parliament. The modern country of England remains distinct from the UK as a whole.

overview.text: The Kingdom of England was a historical monarchy that developed from earlier English kingdoms and lasted until union with Scotland in 1707. Viking pressure helped bring a unified English kingdom into being in the early medieval period. In 1066 William of Normandy defeated King Harold at Hastings and became king, beginning Norman rule. King John faced a baronial rebellion and agreed to Magna Carta at Runnymede in 1215. The charter addressed grievances against royal power, especially those of the barons; it did not create a modern parliament or grant equal rights to everyone. The kingdoms of England and Scotland retained separate parliaments until the 1707 union formed the Kingdom of Great Britain.

key_facts.text: A unified English kingdom emerged during the Viking period.
William of Normandy defeated King Harold at Hastings in 1066.
King John agreed to Magna Carta at Runnymede in 1215.
The original Magna Carta primarily protected baronial interests, not universal rights.
England and Scotland united as Great Britain on May 1, 1707.
The union replaced their separate parliaments with one Parliament of Great Britain.

overview.text: The British Empire was a changing network of colonies and other territories under British rule or influence across several continents. It was built through trade, settlement, military conquest, and coercive colonial administration; its peoples had very different rights and experiences. British imperial power reached southern Africa, where the army invaded the independent Zulu Kingdom in 1879 and later fought the Boer republics from 1899 to 1902. The empire also depended on enslaved labor in Atlantic colonies, although Parliament outlawed the British slave trade in 1807 and emancipation came later. During the First World War, people from India, Africa, the Caribbean, Canada, and Australia served in imperial forces. Independence movements, including India and Pakistan’s in 1947, gradually dismantled imperial rule.

overview.text: Ancient Corinth was a Greek city on the Isthmus of Corinth, the narrow land connection between mainland Greece and the Peloponnese. Its position near routes linking two seas supported trade, colonization, and the export of decorated pottery. Corinth administered the Isthmian Games at nearby Isthmia, a festival honoring Poseidon. Greek tradition named Sisyphus as the city’s legendary founder, though that story is mythology rather than a historical founding record. The city took part in conflicts involving Sparta and Athens and later lent its name to the Corinthian War. Rome sacked Corinth in 146 BCE; Julius Caesar founded a Roman colony at the site in 44 BCE. The later Roman city was visited by the apostle Paul.
